questions.stem: The dynasty that IMMEDIATELY succeeded the Mauryas in Magadha (after the last Mauryan emperor Brihadratha was killed in 185 BCE) was the:
questions.explanation: SHUNGA DYNASTY (185-73 BCE, ~112 years) — founded when PUSHYAMITRA SHUNGA (the Brahmin senapati / commander-in-chief of the Mauryan army) ASSASSINATED the last Mauryan emperor BRIHADRATHA during a military PARADE in Pataliputra in 185 BCE. Pushyamitra Shunga established himself as the new king of Magadha; his capital was PATALIPUTRA. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) End of Mauryan empire, 137 years after Chandragupta Maurya founded it; (2) Began a period of PERIPHERAL INVASIONS and FRAGMENTATION of north India. PUSHYAMITRA SHUNGA: (a) celebrated HINDU REVIVAL after Ashokan Buddhism; reportedly persecuted Buddhists (per Buddhist texts like Ashokavadana/Divyavadana) though historical veracity is debated; (b) performed two ASHVAMEDHA YAJNAS (horse sacrifices) as claimed in Ayodhya inscription; (c) faced Greek (Indo-Greek) invasions — DEMETRIUS of Bactria, then MENANDER I (MILINDA) who reached as far as Sagala (Sialkot); famous ‘MILINDA PANHA’ is dialogue of Milinda with Buddhist monk NAGASENA. (d) Pushyamitra's court patronised Sanskrit: PATANJALI (the grammarian, author of Mahabhashya — commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi) was contemporary — some say court scholar; Patanjali also credited with Yoga Sutras (may be same/different person). Pushyamitra was succeeded by AGNIMITRA (subject of Kalidasa's MALAVIKAGNIMITRAM play, though Kalidasa is much later, 4th-5th century CE), Vasujyestha, Vasumitra, Andhraka, Pulindaka, Ghosha, Vajramitra, Bhagabhadra, Devabhuti (last Shunga, killed ~73 BCE by Vasudeva Kanva of the Kanva dynasty — who then ruled 73-28 BCE for just 45 years). BUILDING legacy: despite alleged anti-Buddhism, Shunga ART FLOURISHED — BHARHUT STUPA (MP) railings and torana, SANCHI STUPA (MP, originally built by Ashoka; enlarged+encased in Shunga period with stone railing); the medallions and reliefs of these stupas are Shunga art (2nd-1st c. BCE). Religious literature: Shunga era is when MANU SMRITI was composed (uncertain, 2nd BCE - 2nd CE); later sections of RAMAYANA + MAHABHARATA + Puranas were compiled. KANVAS succeeded Shungas 73-28 BCE (4 rulers: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, Susarman); then SATAVAHANAS of Deccan swept north and ended them in 28 BCE. founded by PUSHYAMITRA SHUNGA, a Brahmin commander-in-chief of the Mauryan army who killed Brihadratha during a military parade; ruled Magadha ~185-73 BCE.

questions.stem: The SATAVAHANA DYNASTY, which ruled the DECCAN for nearly 4 centuries from ~230 BCE to 220 CE, had its capital at:

options.option_text: PRATISHTHANA (modern PAITHAN on the Godavari river, in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra); also used Amaravati (on Krishna, AP) as secondary capital

questions.explanation: SATAVAHANA DYNASTY (~230 BCE - 220 CE, ~450 years) — the GREATEST early DECCAN dynasty; also known as ANDHRAS (mentioned in Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII as vassals, and in the Puranas as ‘ANDHRAS’ and ‘ANDHRABHRTYAS’). FOUNDER: SIMUKA (c. 230 BCE). CAPITAL: PRATISHTHANA (modern PAITHAN in Maharashtra, on the Godavari, still a pilgrimage site); also AMARAVATI (on Krishna, near Guntur, Andhra Pradesh) was a major political + Buddhist centre; DHANYAKATAKA / Dharanikota nearby. LANGUAGE of records: mostly PRAKRIT (Brahmi script); occasional Sanskrit. DOMAIN: at peak, covered Maharashtra, MP, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Gujarat, Konkan. GREATEST RULERS: (1) SATAKARNI I (c. 70 BCE) — performed 2 Ashvamedhas, 1 Rajasuya; mentioned in NANAGHAT inscription (Naneghat Caves, Maharashtra — where his wife Naganika inscribed his reign). (2) HALA (c. 20-24 CE) — a SCHOLAR-KING; compiled ‘GATHA SAPTASHATI’ / GATHASATTASAI — an ANTHOLOGY of 700 PRAKRIT love poems by various poets; one of oldest Indian literary anthologies. (3) GAUTAMIPUTRA SATAKARNI (c. 106-130 CE) — regarded as the greatest Satavahana; defeated the Saka KSHAHARATA chief NAHAPANA (Kshatrapa satrap) and took back Deccan + Gujarat + Malwa; his mother GAUTAMI BALASHRI composed the NASIK CAVE INSCRIPTION (a eulogy calling him ‘destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas, conqueror of Sakas-Yavanas-Pahlavas’). (4) VASHISHTHIPUTRA PULUMAYI (130-158 CE) — son of Gautamiputra; his coins bear ship images (maritime trade). (5) YAJNA SATAKARNI (c. 170-190 CE) — last strong ruler; after him the empire fragmented; Ikshvakus, Abhiras, Vakatakas, etc., rose. ART & ARCHITECTURE: Satavahanas were great patrons of BUDDHISM (despite being Vedic/Hindu rulers themselves). Built/patronised: (1) AMARAVATI STUPA (AP) — MAHACHAITYA — famous for marble drum-slab reliefs, now mostly in British Museum and Madras Museum. (2) NAGARJUNAKONDA (AP) — Buddhist centre; but peak was under Ikshvakus successor. (3) KARLE, BHAJA, NASIK, KANHERI CAVES — ROCK-CUT BUDDHIST CAVES (chaitya halls + viharas) in Western Ghats; cathedral-like Karla chaitya is stunning. (4) AJANTA — earliest caves (9, 10) begun in Satavahana times (though famous paintings are Vakataka/Gupta era). ECONOMY: issued LEAD, POTIN, COPPER, SILVER coins; controlled Indo-Roman maritime trade via ports (Broach/Bharukaccha, Sopara, Kalyan); Pliny and Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st c. CE Roman text) describe brisk trade in silk, cotton, muslin, spices, ivory, gems. DECLINE: weakened after 2nd c. CE; IKSHVAKUS of AP, ABHIRAS of Maharashtra, VAKATAKAS of Vidarbha, PALLAVAS of Kanchi emerged.

questions.stem: The greatest KUSHANA ruler, under whom Buddhism received royal patronage and the 4th Buddhist Council was held in Kashmir, was:
questions.explanation: KANISHKA I (KANISHKA THE GREAT) — the most famous KUSHANA emperor. Ruled c. 78-144 CE (dates long debated). Kushanas were a branch of the YUEH-CHI tribe (of Central Asian / Chinese origin) who migrated west into Bactria (Afghanistan) and then entered India through the NW. KANISHKA'S EMPIRE: vast — from Central Asia (parts of Tajikistan + Uzbekistan) + Afghanistan + Pakistan + N India down to Mathura + Sanchi + Bihar. CAPITALS: two — PURUSHAPURA (PESHAWAR, Pakistan) + MATHURA (UP). ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) ADOPTED + PATRONISED MAHAYANA BUDDHISM (though Kanishka was tolerant of all — his coins depict Greek + Iranian + Indian deities). (2) CONVENED the 4TH BUDDHIST COUNCIL at KUNDALAVANA (KASHMIR), ~78 CE (or thereabouts); presided by VASUMITRA, with poet-philosopher ASVAGHOSHA as vice-president. This council: (a) compiled Buddhist texts in SANSKRIT (earlier councils in Pali/Magadhi); (b) produced the MAHAVIBHASHA commentary on the Abhidharma; (c) accelerated the rise of MAHAYANA Buddhism over Theravada/Hinayana. (3) STARTED THE SAKA ERA on 22 March 78 CE — still used as INDIA'S NATIONAL CIVIL CALENDAR (SHAKA SAMVAT), adopted officially in 1957; 78 years behind Gregorian. (4) First Indian ruler to issue GOLD COINS (Roman-style, high quality) along with copper coins — gold from Roman trade + Central Asian mines. (5) Patronised BUDDHIST ART — GANDHARA school (Greco-Buddhist hybrid, Afghanistan-Pakistan, wavy hair + Greek robes, standing/seated Buddha statues — first physical representations of Buddha) and MATHURA school (indigenous red-sandstone, kapotaka style). (6) Patronised scholars: ASVAGHOSHA (poet, wrote BUDDHACHARITA + SAUNDARANANDA — Buddhist Sanskrit mahakavyas; first Indian Sanskrit ‘drama’); NAGARJUNA (founder of MADHYAMIKA philosophy + SUNYATA doctrine); VASUMITRA; CHARAKA (physician, author of Charaka Samhita); Mathara/Parsva. (7) KANISHKA'S STUPA at PESHAWAR — one of the tallest stupas of ancient world (reported 13-storey or 400 ft) — contained Buddha relics (excavated 1908, relics now in Burma). (8) Kanishka's HEADLESS STATUE at MATHURA MUSEUM — famously preserved (head broken off by iconoclasts later). INSCRIPTION: RABATAK (discovered 1993 in Afghanistan) — gives GENEALOGY of Kushanas: KUJULA KADPHISES (founder, c. 30-80 CE) → VIMA TAKTO → VIMA KADPHISES → KANISHKA I → HUVISHKA → VASUDEVA I (last great, after whom empire declined). KUSHANAS collapsed after 230 CE due to Sasanian invasions from Persia; smaller Kushano-Sasanian kingdoms continued; remnants absorbed by GUPTAS.

questions.stem: India's NATIONAL CALENDAR, the SAKA ERA, begins from the year:

options.option_text: 78 CE — started by Kushana emperor KANISHKA I; adopted as India’s National Civil Calendar by GoI in 1957, alongside Gregorian; 78 years behind Gregorian

questions.explanation: SAKA SAMVAT / SAKA ERA — INDIA'S NATIONAL CIVIL CALENDAR (Rashtriya Panchang). STARTED: 22 March 78 CE, the traditional date of KANISHKA I's accession / the vernal equinox of that year. Thus Saka Year = Gregorian Year − 78 (for dates after 22 March). E.g., 2026 CE → 1948 Saka; 20 April 2026 → 30 Chaitra 1948 Saka. Saka is BEHIND Gregorian by 78 years. MONTHS of Saka (based on tropical signs of zodiac, 12 months): CHAITRA (Mar-Apr, 30 days; 31 in leap year) → VAISHAKHA → JYESTHA → ASHADHA → SHRAVANA → BHADRA → ASHVIN → KARTIKA → AGRAHAYANA (Margashira) → PAUSHA → MAGHA → PHALGUNA. NEW YEAR's DAY: 1 CHAITRA = 22 March (or 21 March in Gregorian leap years). LEAP YEAR rule same as Gregorian (adds 1 day to Chaitra). ADOPTED on 22 March 1957 by Government of India, alongside Gregorian, based on recommendations of CALENDAR REFORM COMMITTEE (1952) chaired by MEGHNAD SAHA (astrophysicist). Saka dates appear in: (1) Gazette of India; (2) All India Radio (AIR) national news announcements; (3) Government communications; (4) Calendars issued by GoI. OTHER PROMINENT INDIAN ERAS: (I) VIKRAMA SAMVAT (VS) — started 58/57 BCE; traditionally by King VIKRAMADITYA of Ujjain after defeating Sakas; used in N India, Nepal (official Nepali calendar Bikram Sambat). 2026 CE = 2083 VS. (II) KALI YUGA — started 3102 BCE (traditional Hindu astronomical era); age of Kali (4,32,000 years); current year 5127 (2026). (III) GUPTA ERA — 319/320 CE (start of Chandragupta I's reign); used in Gupta + Vakataka inscriptions. (IV) HARSHA ERA — 606 CE (start of Harshavardhana's reign). (V) HIJRI (ISLAMIC) — 622 CE (Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina); lunar; 622 CE = 1 AH; 2026 CE ≈ 1447-1448 AH. (VI) BUDDHIST ERA — 544/543 BCE (Buddha's Mahaparinirvana by Theravada reckoning); 2026 CE = 2569 BE. (VII) BANGLA SAMBAT / Bengali calendar — 594 CE (claimed link to King Shashanka of Gauda, or revised by Akbar from Islamic era); 2026 CE = 1432-1433 BS; 14/15 April = Pohela Boishakh (Bengali New Year). (VIII) KOLLAM ERA — 825 CE, used in Kerala (Kollavarsham). (IX) SAPTA-RISHI era — used in Kashmir. GLOBAL CIVIL CALENDAR: GREGORIAN, introduced 15 Oct 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII (reformed Julian calendar of Julius Caesar 46 BCE). India followed British adoption in 1752 (when UK finally shifted). Leap year rule: every 4 yrs, except century years not divisible by 400 (so 1900 NOT leap, 2000 LEAP, 2100 NOT leap).

questions.stem: The INDO-GREEK ruler MENANDER I (MILINDA, c. 165-130 BCE), remembered for his dialogue with Buddhist monk NAGASENA, had his capital at:
questions.explanation: MENANDER I SOTER (‘Saviour’) / MILINDA (c. 165-130 BCE) — greatest INDO-GREEK ruler. Indo-Greeks (also called Yavanas in Sanskrit) were successors of ALEXANDER THE GREAT's conquests of Bactria (Afghanistan) + NW India. They established kingdoms in Bactria (c. 250 BCE by DIODOTUS) and later spread into India. Menander ruled from SAGALA (modern SIALKOT, Punjab, Pakistan). EMPIRE: stretched from Bactria + Arachosia to Gandhara + Taxila + Punjab + as far east as Mathura. He is CELEBRATED in Buddhist literature as a CONVERT TO BUDDHISM. The ‘MILINDA PANHA’ (‘QUESTIONS OF MILINDA’) is a famous PALI text (1st c. BCE or later) recording a series of DIALOGUES between King Milinda and the Buddhist sage NAGASENA on doctrinal questions — self, soul, rebirth, nirvana; one of the best-known Indian Buddhist non-canonical works. Like the dialogues of Socrates, but in Buddhist philosophical tradition. Menander's COINS (bilingual, Greek + Kharoshthi; silver drachms) have been found widely. GREEK HISTORIAN STRABO claimed Menander's conquests ‘exceeded even those of Alexander’. Menander also sent ambassadors and had contact with Central Asia. After his death (130 BCE), his empire began to fragment; his widow Agathokleia served as regent for his son Strato I. Other notable Indo-Greek kings: DEMETRIUS I (‘king of India’), ANTIALKIDAS (sent HELIODORUS as envoy to SHUNGA king at Vidisha — Heliodorus converted to Bhagavata Vaishnavism and erected the HELIODORUS PILLAR at Besnagar/Vidisha, MP, with Garuda, dedicated to Vasudeva-Krishna — one of earliest evidence of devotional Vaishnavism). INDO-GREEKS were eventually displaced by: (1) SAKAS / Scythians (Indo-Scythians, from Central Asia, c. 1st c. BCE; MAUES was first king); (2) PAHLAVAS / Parthians; (3) KUSHANAS (Yueh-Chi). Indo-Greeks RETREATED to Hindu Kush by c. 10 CE. CULTURAL IMPACT: Hellenistic art + GANDHARAN sculpture (Greco-Buddhist style — Buddha depicted with Apollo-like features, wavy hair, toga-drapes); ASTRONOMY (Indian astronomy borrowed zodiac signs — Rashi names like Mesha = Aries, Vrishabha = Taurus — from Greek); GEOMETRY; COINAGE (Indian kings adopted Greek coin design conventions); POSSIBLY Indian theatre structure (though disputed). The ‘YAVANAS’ / ‘YAVANI’ script/language (= Greek) is mentioned in Patanjali's Mahabhashya and Kamasutra. Rock edicts of Ashoka mention Greek kings Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Magas, Antigonus, Alexander as recipients of his dhamma messengers. Thus Indo-Greeks bridged the cross-cultural Indo-Mediterranean exchange for ~250 years. ruled over most of NW India down to Mathura; the dialogue forms the ‘MILINDA PANHA’ (Questions of Milinda) in Pali, a Buddhist classic; SIALKOT, Punjab, Pakistan.

questions.stem: The art school famous for its HELLENISTIC / GRAECO-BUDDHIST style, depicting the Buddha with WAVY HAIR and GRECIAN ROBES, is the:

options.option_text: GANDHARA SCHOOL — flourished in present-day NW Pakistan + E Afghanistan; 1st-5th c. CE; Greek-Roman + Indian + Central Asian fusion; patronised under Kushanas (esp. Kanishka); first physical Buddha images here

questions.explanation: GANDHARA SCHOOL OF ART (1st c. BCE - 5th c. CE) — one of three great SCHOOLS OF INDIAN BUDDHIST ART (along with Mathura + Amaravati). Named after the region GANDHARA (modern TAKHT-I-BAHI, Peshawar, Swat, Taxila in Pakistan + parts of E Afghanistan). DEFINING FEATURES: (1) HELLENISTIC GRECO-ROMAN INFLUENCE due to Indo-Greek presence + exposure to Roman trade + Kushana patronage; (2) BUDDHA STATUES with APOLLO-LIKE face (oval, sharp nose, wavy curly hair, serene gaze, half-closed meditative eyes); (3) drapery — TOGA-STYLE FLOWING ROBES (sanghati) with heavy folds (imitating Greek/Roman sculpture); (4) HALOS (nimbus) behind head — derived from sun-god imagery; (5) anatomically realistic body (Greek human proportions); (6) MATERIAL: grey-black SCHIST stone (Gandhara) + later STUCCO + terracotta. LEADING SITES: (a) TAKHT-I-BAHI (Pakistan, UNESCO WHS 1980) — rock-cut Buddhist monastery; (b) TAXILA (Pakistan, UNESCO WHS 1980) — includes Dharmarajika Stupa, Sirkap city, Sirsukh, Jaulian, Mohra Moradu monasteries; (c) SWAT VALLEY (Butkara, Saidu Sharif); (d) HADDA + BAMIYAN (Afghanistan) — the BAMIYAN BUDDHAS (2 colossal Buddhas, 6th c. CE, 53 m + 35 m tall) were destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001 — one of the great cultural losses of our time. Reconstruction debated. PATRONS: (I) Indo-Greeks + Indo-Scythian rulers; (II) KUSHANAS — esp. KANISHKA I + HUVISHKA (2nd c. CE) — the golden age of Gandhara. MATHURA SCHOOL (2nd c. BCE - 7th c. CE) — contemporary, INDIGENOUS SCHOOL centred at Mathura (UP). Features: (a) RED SANDSTONE from Sikri/Kasupa quarries; (b) INDIAN aesthetic — fuller body, CURLY KNOT OF HAIR (USHNISHA), URNA (mark between brows), earlobe elongation, erect posture, smiling face, THINNER-TRANSPARENT drapery (not layered like Gandhara); (c) depicted not just Buddha but JAIN tirthankaras, Hindu gods (Krishna, Shiva), and KUSHANA PORTRAIT sculptures (famous HEADLESS KANISHKA statue); (d) developed iconographic conventions that became Pan-Indian (lotus seat, mudras, parasol); (e) mass-production of images that travelled widely. AMARAVATI SCHOOL (2nd c. BCE - 3rd c. CE) — in the DECCAN, patronised by SATAVAHANAS + IKSHVAKUS. Features: (a) WHITE LIMESTONE / MARBLE; (b) narrative reliefs on stupa DRUM-SLABS showing Jataka tales + Buddha's life; (c) dynamic poses, slender graceful bodies, crowded compositions; (d) early aniconic (symbols — footprints, empty throne) transitioning to anthropomorphic Buddha. AMARAVATI STUPA reliefs now in British Museum (London) + Government Museum Chennai + Amaravati Archaeological Museum. OTHER SCHOOLS that emerged later: SARNATH (late Gupta), PALA (Bihar-Bengal, 8-12th c.), HOYSALA (Karnataka, 11-14th c.).

questions.stem: RUDRADAMAN I, the Shaka (Western Kshatrapa) ruler of Saurashtra, is famous for the:
questions.explanation: JUNAGADH ROCK INSCRIPTION of RUDRADAMAN I (150 CE) — inscribed on the same ROCK near GIRNAR HILL (Junagadh, Gujarat) that already carried Ashoka's earlier rock edicts. Considered the EARLIEST LONG SANSKRIT INSCRIPTION (earlier Sanskrit inscriptions are much shorter). CONTENTS: (1) Records in chaste Sanskrit (influenced by Panini's grammar; kavya style with poetry + prose alternating) the REPAIR of the SUDARSHANA LAKE (Reservoir) — originally built by PUSHYAGUPTA, a Mauryan viceroy under CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA (4th c. BCE), improved by YAVANA (Greek) governor TUSHASPHA under ASHOKA (3rd c. BCE); the dam had BURST due to storm/flood; Rudradaman had it rebuilt on grander scale ~150 CE without levying fresh tax on his subjects. (2) PRAISES Rudradaman's achievements: defeated Yaudheyas, Satakarni king TWICE (but spared out of kinship — Rudradaman's daughter was married to Vasishthiputra Satakarni's son). (3) Calls Rudradaman a MASTER OF THE SACRED (Brahmanical) + SECULAR SCIENCES, grammar, rhetoric, music, logic, statesmanship — a renaissance-man king. Significance: (a) shows RESURGENCE OF SANSKRIT as an inscriptional/administrative language (for 5 centuries Prakrit had dominated epigraphy — Ashoka, Satavahanas, Kharavela); (b) reveals Shaka Kshatrapa statecraft; (c) indicates water management + public works continued Mauryan tradition. RUDRADAMAN I (c. 130-150 CE) — grandson of CHASHTANA (who founded the W Kshatrapa line c. 78 CE; Chashtana mentioned in Ptolemy's Geography as ‘Tiastenes’). Western Kshatrapas were a branch of SAKAS who ruled W India (Gujarat, Kathiawar, Malwa, Sindh, Rajasthan) c. 35-415 CE; contemporaries of Satavahanas + Kushanas + later Guptas. Rudradaman's empire: Saurashtra, Kutch, Sindh, Malwa, Konkan. He was the most powerful Shaka ruler; his SILVER coinage (following Greek standard, 2.2 g) set trend for long. Western Kshatrapas ended when CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA of Guptas conquered Rudrasimha III in ~415 CE. OTHER IMPORTANT SANSKRIT INSCRIPTIONS of this broad era: (1) ALLAHABAD PILLAR / PRAYAG PRASHASTI of SAMUDRAGUPTA (c. 350 CE) — by HARISHENA; reuses the same Ashoka pillar. (2) AIHOLE inscription of Pulakeshin II (by RAVIKIRTI, Chalukya court poet, 634 CE) — records victory over Harsha. (3) MANDASOR inscription of YASHODHARMAN (c. 532 CE) — commemorates defeat of Hun king MIHIRAKULA. (4) BHITARI PILLAR of Skandagupta — records Hun defeat. (5) HATHIGUMPHA inscription of KHARAVELA of KALINGA at Udayagiri (Bhubaneshwar, Odisha) — but this one is in Prakrit (not Sanskrit), ~1st c. BCE.

questions.stem: The SANGAM AGE of Tamil literature flourished in the FAR SOUTH (Tamilakam) approximately during which period?
questions.explanation: SANGAM AGE — classical age of TAMIL literature + history; named after SANGAMS (Tamil ‘Sangam’ means assembly/academy — from Sanskrit ‘Sangha’). Traditional Tamil legend speaks of THREE SANGAMS held at Madurai/Kapatapuram under the PANDYA patronage: First Sangam — 4,400 years, lost to a deluge; Second Sangam — 3,700 years, also lost; Third Sangam — 1,850 years, whose output SURVIVED. The Third Sangam (~3rd c. BCE to 3rd c. CE) is what scholars identify as the historical Sangam period. CONTEMPORARY to: Mauryas (their mention in Sangam poems + Ashoka's edict II and XIII referring to south Indian kingdoms), Satavahanas, Sakas. LOCATION: TAMILAKAM — comprised modern Tamil Nadu, Kerala, parts of Karnataka + Andhra; also Sri Lanka had presence. THREE DYNASTIES: (I) CHERAS — west coast (Kerala + west TN); capital VANJI (later KARUR); emblem BOW; greatest king SENGUTTUVAN (‘the Just’) — hero of SILAPPADIKARAM; performed Aryan-influenced ceremonies + led expedition to Himalayas to get stone for KANNAGI (the chaste wife) statue. (II) CHOLAS — central TN, Kaveri delta; capitals UPHUR + KAVERIPOOMPATTINAM / PUHAR (port); emblem TIGER; greatest: KARIKALA (‘the one with the charred leg’) — defeated Cheras + Pandyas at battle of Venni, built the GRAND ANICUT (Kallanai dam across Kaveri, ~1st-2nd c. CE — oldest functional DAM in the world still in use). (III) PANDYAS — southern TN + Kerala; capital MADURAI; emblem FISH; presided over the Tamil Sangams; known for pearl fishery of Korkai port. SANGAM LITERATURE — ~473 poets, ~2,381 poems survive; in ancient Tamil (before Brahmi adaptation to Tamil-Brahmi script). DIVIDED INTO: (I) ETTUTHOKAI (‘Eight Anthologies’) — AKANANURU (love poetry on ‘akam’ — inner life); PURANANURU (heroic/public poetry on ‘puram’); NARRINAI; KURUNTOKAI; KALITOKAI; AINKURUNURU; PARIPATAL; PATIRRUPPATTU. (II) PATTUPPATTU (‘Ten Idylls’) — long narrative poems incl. TIRUMURUGARRUPPATAI, POR UNARATRUPPATAI, MALAIPATUKATAM. (III) PATINENKILKANAKKU (18 minor works) — shorter; includes TIRUKKURAL by TIRUVALLUVAR (!!! though most scholars date Kural to post-Sangam 4-5th c. CE). (IV) TWO GREAT EPICS (later, c. 5th-6th CE but part of extended Sangam tradition): SILAPPADIKARAM (‘The Tale of the Anklet’) by ILANGO ADIGAL — heroine Kannagi, husband Kovalan murdered unjustly by Pandya king, she burns Madurai down; MANIMEKALAI by SATTANAR — Buddhist, sequel about Kovalan's daughter Manimekalai. Plus JIVAKA-CHINTAMANI (Jain, by Tiruttakkadevar) + SILAPPADIKARAM + VALAIYAPATI + KUNDALAKESI = ‘FIVE GREAT EPICS of Tamil’. CULTURE from Sangam: 5 TINAIS (landscape types — kurinji hills, mullai forest/pastoral, marudam farmland, neydal seashore, palai arid); each associated with specific deity + mood of love. Religion: a mix of indigenous Tamil worship + later-adopted Hindu deities + Jain + Buddhist presence (Nagarjunakonda, Amaravati). After Sangam era: KALABHRA interregnum (3rd-6th c.), then PALLAVAS rose + Pandya revival + Early Cholas. roughly parallel to the post-Mauryan / Satavahana period in the north; ‘Sangam’ = assembly of poets/scholars under Pandya patronage; produced a vast body of secular Tamil poetry.

questions.stem: The GRAND ANICUT (Kallanai), regarded as one of the OLDEST WATER-DIVERSION STRUCTURES in the world STILL IN USE, was built by:

options.option_text: KARIKALA CHOLA (c. 1st-2nd c. CE) across the KAVERI RIVER near TIRUCHIRAPPALLI, Tamil Nadu
Rajaraja Chola I in the 11th century

questions.explanation: GRAND ANICUT / KALLANAI (Tamil ‘kal’ = stone + ‘anai’ = dam) — ancient water-diversion dam across the KAVERI (Cauvery) RIVER at a point where the river branches into many distributaries, near TIRUCHIRAPPALLI (modern Trichy), Tamil Nadu. BUILT BY: KARIKALA CHOLA — greatest EARLY CHOLA king, SANGAM AGE; c. 1st-2nd century CE (exact date debated; could be 2nd c. BCE to 2nd c. CE). STRUCTURE: originally ~329 m (1,080 ft) LONG, ~20 m wide, ~5 m high; built of LARGE STONES (unhewn granite) packed together without mortar; engineered to REGULATE Kaveri waters into 4 distributaries, prevent floods, and irrigate the KAVERI DELTA agricultural heartland. STILL IN USE today, 2,000 years later — one of the OLDEST WATER-ENGINEERING structures on Earth still in regular service (probably only the MARIB DAM of Yemen 8th c. BCE is older; that one collapsed). British engineer Sir Arthur Cotton (who built LOWER ANICUT + modern Dowleswaram dam) studied and ADMIRED the Grand Anicut; incorporated its principles into the UPPER ANICUT (1836-38). Today the Kallanai is a protected ancient monument; enlarged Mettur Dam (1934) upstream + modern works. The Kaveri delta it irrigates is called the ‘RICE BOWL OF SOUTH INDIA’ — produces 3 crops/year. OTHER ANCIENT INDIAN WATER ENGINEERING: (1) SUDARSHANA LAKE at Girnar (Gujarat) — Mauryan period, repaired by Rudradaman (as per Junagadh inscription). (2) Indus Valley DOCKS at LOTHAL (2400 BCE) + water reservoirs at DHOLAVIRA (world's first known rainwater harvesting system with 16 reservoirs, step-wells). (3) Vijayanagara's extensive canal + tank systems including KAMALAPUR tank, ANANTARAJA TANK. (4) KAREZ / QANAT underground water channels (Persia + Deccan sultanates). (5) KAIL HAUZ / BAOLIS (stepwells) of Delhi, Gujarat (RANI KI VAV at Patan, UNESCO WHS — 11th c. Solanki), Rajasthan (CHAND BAORI, ADI KUMBESHWARA). (6) BHOJPAL / BHOJ TAL of Bhopal — built by Raja Bhoja of Malwa, 11th century. (7) BASTI in Karnataka — Jain temple reservoirs. KARIKALA CHOLA also conquered Chera + Pandya + fought to defeat; his fame is such that even Rajaraja Chola I (11th c.) referred to himself as Karikala's ‘descendant’. His capital was KAVERIPATTINAM / PUHAR — a great trading port (destroyed by a tsunami later, as per Tamil tradition; Roman amphorae + ceramics have been excavated there). Karikala also celebrated in SANGAM poetry — PORUNARATRUPPATTAI (a pattuppattu) extols him. ~329 m long stone dam; still functional after ~2,000 years; irrigates ~10 lakh acres of Kaveri delta.

questions.stem: KHARAVELA, the great ruler of KALINGA who commissioned the HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION at Udayagiri (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), belonged to the:
questions.explanation: KHARAVELA (c. 193-170 BCE or 1st century BCE per modern scholarship) — greatest ruler of the MAHAMEGHAVAHANA / CHEDI dynasty of KALINGA (modern ODISHA). CAPITAL: KALINGANAGARI (near modern Bhubaneswar/Puri). JAINISM was his state religion — Kharavela was a devout JAIN (he recovered the JAIN image of ‘Kalinga Jina’ that Magadha king had taken during Mahapadma Nanda's raids centuries earlier, +other Jain relics). HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION (‘Cave of the Elephant’ — named after its entrance) at UDAYAGIRI HILL, near Bhubaneswar, Odisha. One of the MOST IMPORTANT INSCRIPTIONS of ancient India. Inscribed in PRAKRIT (not Sanskrit); in BRAHMI SCRIPT; 17 lines; a PRASHASTI / eulogistic autobiography of Kharavela's reign year by year (up to 13 regnal years). Key content: (1) His military campaigns — defeated the SATAKARNI (Satavahana king), demarkated MATHURA (defeated some Yavana king), even reached GORATHAGIRI and captured RAJAGRIHA; (2) campaign to MAGADHA defeating its king BAHASATIMITRA / BRIHASPATIMITRA (identified by some scholars with Pushyamitra Shunga — though dates may not align); (3) brought back the JINA idol stolen by NANDAS; (4) public works — construction of canals, aqueducts, subsidies for 35 lakh Brahmins + ascetics; (5) religious + artistic patronage — theatrical performances, music, dance in court; (6) ‘GITA-VADITA-SAMSKITA-NRTYA’ — promotion of GANDHARVA-VEDA (music-dance); (7) convened a council of Jain ASCETICS at KUMARI PARVATA (Udayagiri-Khandagiri hills). Udayagiri-Khandagiri HILLS have ~18+15 = 33 caves hewn as shelters for Jain monks — Hathigumpha, Ranigumpha, Ganesh Gumpha, Swargapuri-Manchapuri, Bagha Gumpha, Sarpa Gumpha — famous as early examples of ROCK-CUT CAVE architecture in E India (~1st c. BCE). Decorated with ELEPHANT, TIGER, SERPENT motifs — precursors to later Chaitya style. JAINISM's three greatest royal patrons in ancient India: (a) CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA — converted to Jainism under BHADRABAHU in old age, migrated with him to Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) + fasted to death (Sallekhana). (b) KHARAVELA — as above. (c) Later, CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA was tolerant but Hindu (Vaishnava); AMOGHAVARSHA I of RASHTRAKUTAS (9th c.) — famous as a Jain king who composed ‘KAVIRAJAMARGA’ in Kannada + renounced throne at end of life to become Jain monk. (d) SOUTH INDIAN Jain renaissance under GANGAS + HOYSALAS + WESTERN CHALUKYAS: BAHUBALI (GOMATESHWARA) statue at SHRAVANABELAGOLA (Karnataka, 57 ft, 981 CE) built by Chamundaraya, Ganga minister; Mahamastakabhisheka every 12 years. (e) CHANDELLAS + RAJPUTS patronised JAIN TEMPLES (Khajuraho Parshvanatha, Osian, Ranakpur (UNESCO Jain temple 1439 CE — 1,444 pillars), Dilwara at Mount Abu (11th-13th c. — marble craftsmanship), Palitana (Satrunjaya hill, 863 temples). ruled Kalinga c. 1st century BCE; Kharavela was a JAIN, patronised Jainism; Hathigumpha inscription is his famous prashasti.
